headline: The Games That Tell Palestine’s Story: A Fight to Keep Heritage Alive
snippet: JENIN, West Bank / PNN — In an effort to prevent traditional Palestinian games from being forgotten, Samahear Al-Roumi, director of the “Bayt Al-Dammah” centre for reviving Palestinian folk games in the town of Zababdeh in Jenin governorate, is documenting the games, introducing them to younger generations and reconnecting them with the history, culture, customs and traditions of Palestinian towns and villages. Al-Roumi said Bayt Al-Dammah was established as a space dedicated to preserving Palestinian folk games from disappearing, explaining that the project brings together three main categories of traditional games. The first category includes games that rely on thinking and strategy, such as Al-Dammah, Al-Sijah and Mancala. The second consists of movement-based games, including Seven Stones, Abu Asfourah, also known as Al-Habi, Al-Hila and Hopscotch. Al-Roumi noted that some games are known by different names in different parts of Palestine. The third category includes games that document Palestinian cities and villages that were depopulated, with each game linked to a particular city and the villages associated with it. Among them are games representing Acre and its villages, Haifa and its villages, Safed and others. A game with a story and a lesson Al-Roumi said every game at Bayt Al-Dammah carries information and a story connected to a particular place and to Palestinian heritage, helping visitors learn about their own villages or cities, as well as their culture and traditions. She cited the example of the Olive Press game, which is linked to an olive press in Sebastia, known for its olive trees and traditional olive presses. Through the game, visitors first learn about the history of the place before playing it themselves. The aim, she said, goes beyond simply playing traditional games. Instead, the project seeks to turn each game into a gateway to Palestinian history, geography and heritage. Al-Roumi said the design and colours of Bayt Al-Dammah were inspired by the oranges of Haifa and Jaffa, adding that the centre seeks to create a space where Palestinian visitors can experience a connection with the simpler way of life that existed decades ago. She described it as a return to a time when Palestinians relied heavily on local resources, surrounded by mulberry, fig and pomegranate trees and za'atar, as well as wells and small farms — reflecting a rural way of life built largely on self-reliance. Shortlisted among hundreds of projects Al-Roumi said Bayt Al-Dammah was selected from among 293 projects and reached the qualifying stage of an event in Jordan attended by Princess Dana Firas. The project was also documented in a dedicated festival catalogue. Every Sunday afternoon, Bayt Al-Dammah welcomes children and their mothers, allowing them to play traditional games together. The centre also accepts bookings from institutions, charities, universities and other organisations wishing to organise visits or activities. The project’s activities are not confined to the centre. Al-Roumi said the games can also be transported and used at festivals, conferences and other events. Older generations discover games they never knew were Palestinian The surprise is not limited to children, Al-Roumi said. Some visitors over the age of 50 have discovered for the first time that games they encounter at Bayt Al-Dammah are, in fact, longstanding Palestinian folk games. The initiative introduces visitors to the history of the games, some of which date back to earlier historical periods. Others were introduced to the Levant during the Ottoman era. Each game has its own history and context, which the centre's management explains to visitors. Bayt Al-Dammah also sells a number of Palestinian traditional games in an effort to keep them present in homes and among children and younger generations, rather than limiting their use to heritage events. From traditional preservation to digital archiving Al-Roumi said preserving Palestinian folk games requires moving towards a new stage of documentation. She highlighted the need to produce a specialised catalogue of Palestinian traditional games containing the games themselves, their rules, their history and information about the Palestinian regions with which they are associated. She also stressed the importance of digitally archiving the games, calling on universities and specialist students — including students and graduates in artificial intelligence — to work with the project to document and preserve the games through digital tools capable of bringing Palestinian heritage to a wider audience around the world. The project's primary goal, she said, is to prevent Palestinian folk games from disappearing because they form part of Palestinian memory, culture and identity, and to pass them from one generation to another through practice, documentation and an understanding of their history. **This video was produced with financial support from CFI, Expertise France and the European Union. headline: India’s steel production clocks 3.7 pc growth at 81.8 million tonnes in H1 2026-27
snippet: New Delhi, Oct 6 (IANS) India’s production of finished steel increased by 3.7 per cent to 81.8 million tonnes during the first half of the current financial year (April-September), compared with the corresponding figure of 78.8 million tonnes in the same period last year, according to data released by the Ministry of Steel on Tuesday. The country’s consumption of finished steel shot up by a robust 7.9 per cent to 84.9 million tonnes during the first half (H1) of 2026-27 from 79 million tonnes in the same period of the last financial year, as demand from big ticket infrastructure projects taken up by the government in the highways, railways and port sectors fuelled demand. India’s steel exports also surged by 26.2 per cent during the first half of the current financial year to 3.55 million tonnes compared with the corresponding figure of 2.81 million tonnes in April-Sept of the previous financial year. In value terms, the exports during April-September jumped by 28.9 per cent to Rs 28,263.7 crore from Rs 21,931.5 crore in the same period last year. Custom Ad: Multiplex The country’s production of crude steel was recorded at 85.1 million tonnes in April-September of the current financial year, compared with 82.7 million tonnes in the same period of the previous year, which represents a 2.9 per cent increase. India's total crude steelmaking capacity currently stands at 222.9 million tonnes per annum, keeping the industry on track to achieve the National Steel Policy target of 300 million tonnes per annum by 2030, according to an official statement. Meanwhile, mining giant NMDC's iron ore production rose 8 per cent year-on-year to 4.04 million tonnes in September 2026, taking the H1 FY 2026–27 output to 27.3 million tonnes, up nearly 23 per cent over H1 FY 2025–26 -- keeping the company on track towards its annual production targets, the statement said. NMDC has commissioned its 2 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) pellet plant at Nagarnar, Chhattisgarh, completing its Rs 5,427-crore integrated project. The project comprises an iron ore processing plant at Bacheli, a 135-km, 15 MTPA slurry pipeline and the Nagarnar pellet plant, which uses Straight Grate Induration technology. It will enable value addition from Bailadila iron ore fines and slimes, reduce road transport of ore and strengthen NMDC's presence across the iron ore value chain. The Ministry of Steel has decided to set up a Steel Industry Safety Council (SISC), an apex body chaired by the Secretary, Ministry of Steel, to strengthen safety standards, accident prevention and safety culture across the steel industry. A dedicated Steel Industry Safety Directorate (SISD) will support the Council through safety audits, investigation of serious incidents and issuance of safety standards suited to Indian conditions, covering iron and steel producers and CPSE mines, the official statement added. --IANS sps/na

headline: Myanmar drug cartels fuel Northeast narcotics threat, exploit unrest to expand network
snippet: New Delhi, Oct 6 (IANS) The fight against narcotics smuggling remains an ongoing challenge, with new threats emerging for Indian agencies with each passing day. Drug cartels operating from Pakistan have come under sustained pressure as the Narendra Modi government at the Centre steps up its efforts to make India drug-free. However, agencies say that despite significant success in dismantling networks linked to operators such as Dawood Ibrahim and Haji Salim, the northeastern states remain a major challenge. The region’s porous borders and difficult terrain continue to provide opportunities for drug traffickers and their networks. An official said that India’s border with Myanmar is the biggest challenge. The ban on the cultivation of opium in Afghanistan by the Taliban regime opened the doors for the cartels operating in Myanmar. “Today Myanmar reportedly produces the largest quantity of opium in the world. Statistics show that in the year 2025, the cultivation area of opium rose to 53,100 hectares,” the official said. Custom Ad: Multiplex The Indian agencies like the Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) and the Assam Rifles continue to work closely, and this has led to major drug busts in the last two to three years. However, narcotics continue to enter India in large quantities. The cultivation of opium in Myanmar remains a challenge beyond India’s direct control. India and Myanmar have held several rounds of talks on the issue and agreed to work together to combat the menace. Officials, however, say tackling the problem will take time, given the enormous scale at which drug cartels operate in Myanmar. Another official said Myanmar’s drug cartels are vast and have access to enormous financial resources. “There is a strong possibility that the combined wealth of these cartels could be significantly greater than that of a government,” the official said. This adds to the challenge for Indian agencies. Even when agencies succeed in busting multiple consignments linked to these cartels, the networks can quickly regroup and establish new supply chains, officials said. Their vast financial resources allow them to absorb losses and continue operations with relative ease. An Intelligence Bureau official said the cartels have repeatedly sought to exploit conflicts and unrest in the northeastern states, particularly Manipur. According to the official, such situations provide drug networks with opportunities to expand their operations and strengthen their presence in the region. On many occasions, investigations have revealed that these cartels have hired their cronies in these states to rake up sensitive issues deliberately so that violence breaks out. The scale of the violence is also huge and runs into several days or even months. This keeps the security agencies completely focused on the violence and how to curb it. The cartels take advantage of this situation and move their consignments into the northeast in large numbers, the official said. In 2025, the NCB had called the scale of the narcotics trade emerging out of Myanmar as ‘dramatic.’ In March 2026, the government told the Lok Sabha that the number of seizures had gone up considerably. In Assam and Tripura, the seizures reported were 31,706 kg and 46,346 kg respectively. In Mizoram, the seizures increased from 1,967 kg in 2024 to 2,233 kg in 2025. Mizoram, on the other hand, saw a major spike in seizures. In 2024, just 284 kilograms of narcotics had been seized. However, the year 2025 recorded 2,556 kg being seized. Officials say that the seizures are no doubt huge. However, the problem persists. Intelligence reports clearly show the cartels have ramped up production in 2026 by nearly three times. This adds to the challenge, as the problem that the agencies are dealing with is huge owing to the quantity of drugs being produced. While Myanmar’s drug cartels have helped make the country one of the world’s largest sources of illicit opium, they are also producing synthetic drugs on a large scale. The growing flow of synthetic drugs from Myanmar into Indian markets poses a major challenge for enforcement agencies. Methamphetamine, in particular, is being smuggled into India in large quantities, driven by strong demand in the domestic market. Custom Ad: Multiplex The agencies are not only battling the scale at which the drugs are being produced and smuggled into the Indian markets. They also face immense challenges when it comes to the terrain in which they are operating. The Moreh-Tamu border is the key transit point for the narcotics cartels. Further adding to the challenge are the porous stretches on the India-Myanmar border and also the forest and hilly terrain, which makes operations for the Indian agencies extremely challenging, an official said. --IANS vn/snj/skp
